system.name: SelfCite
system.one_liner: A self-supervised reward for LLM citations from context ablation: removing the cited text should drop the response probability, keeping only it should hold it.

content.variant_note: one generation step feeds three parallel scoring rows (full context, cited removed, only cited) that fan in to a two-term reward, shown on one cactus example
content.argues: A citation can be rewarded without human labels: its necessity is the probability drop when it is removed, its sufficiency the probability hold when it stands alone.
content.subject: Computing the SelfCite reward for one question, context and response from three language-model probabilities.

elements.name: Generated response (R)
elements.role: the response; the statement r that carries the citation is highlighted

elements.name: Citation E is generated for a specific statement r

elements.drawn_as: cyan text with a curved cyan arrow from the highlighted span

elements.name: Prob. of statement r with C + Q
elements.role: probability of the same statement given the full context: 0.97
elements.drawn_as: pale blue box with a label line and a formula strip with the value in blue

elements.name: Prob. of statement r with C\E + Q
elements.role: probability after removing the cited sentences: 0.01
elements.drawn_as: pale blue box with the value in red and a red-tinted book emoji

elements.name: Prob. of statement r with E + Q
elements.role: probability with only the cited sentences: 0.98
elements.drawn_as: pale blue box with the value in green and a green-tinted book emoji

elements.name: Necessity Score
elements.role: probability drop = 0.97 - 0.01; a large drop means the citation is necessary
elements.drawn_as: light red rounded box with the arithmetic and a small up arrow with a note

elements.name: Sufficiency Score
elements.role: probability hold = 0.98 - 0.97; a more positive value means the citation is sufficient
elements.drawn_as: light green rounded box with the arithmetic and a small up arrow with a note

elements.name: SelfCite Reward = Necessity Score + Sufficiency Score
elements.role: the final reward is the sum of the two scores
elements.drawn_as: bold headline equation with Necessity in red and Sufficiency in green

new_tags.name: emoji-as-variable-symbols

lessons.what_to_learn: To show a reward that compares one quantity under several conditions, redraw the same input card once per condition with coloured bars over what is removed, then carry each condition's colour into its number, its score box and the final equation; emoji can stand in for variables to keep formulas short.
lessons.suits: Reward, metric or ablation-based scoring methods that compare a model's output under modified inputs (removal, masking, perturbation) on one worked example.

evidence: The SelfCite framework calculates rewards based on two metrics: necessity score (probability drop) and sufficiency score (probability hold).
the framework evaluates the probability of generating the same response after (1) removing the cited sentences
their sum is used as the final reward

summary: SelfCite aligns LLMs to cite sentences by rewarding citations through context ablation. Figure 1 computes that reward on one cactus example. A grey context-and-query card is run through a LLaMA box to generate a response whose cited statement is highlighted in cyan. The same card is then redrawn twice: once with the cited sentences covered by red bars, once with only them kept (the others covered in green). Each version gets a probability box with the formula and value for the same statement, 0.97, 0.01 and 0.98, written with emoji for context, query and statement. Curved red and green arrows turn these numbers into a necessity score (probability drop, 0.97 - 0.01) and a sufficiency score (probability hold, 0.98 - 0.97), which are summed into the SelfCite reward.
summary_zh: SelfCite 用上下文消融给引用打分。图 1 以仙人掌问答为例：同一张上下文加问题的卡片画三遍（原文、去掉被引句、只留被引句），各配一个概率框（0.97、0.01、0.98），红绿曲线箭头算出必要性分数和充分性分数，二者相加即奖励。
notes: Prior primary kind stage-pipeline kept; worked-walkthrough added because the figure follows one concrete example with real numbers, and the context card is redrawn per condition. In the third card the green bars sit over the non-cited sentences (read from their position); the red bars in the second card sit over the cited ones.
